listing_view.reasoning: Nothing in what I was given supports pricing, demand, grey market, anchor or subscription evidence — the offer hasn't opened and no basis-for-price chapter was provided, so the seller's document gives no grounds to claim cheapness. What does exist is a deteriorating earnings trend and a 7.6% ROE in the latest year, which is weak cover for any valuation an IPO typically demands. Slight tilt negative because the fundamentals give a buyer no defensive story, but I genuinely cannot see the pricing.

longterm_view.reasoning: The latest year shows revenue down ~24%, PAT down from ₹2,338m to ₹1,320m, ROCE halving to 10.6% and ROE falling to 7.6% — a 7.6% return on equity is below what equity itself costs. Operating cash flow was negative ₹1,970m in the latest year after negative ₹3,186m the year before, meaning reported profit has not been arriving as cash, and receivables stretching from 35 to 137 days says the income statement is increasingly IOUs. The only offsets are a near-ungeared balance sheet (D/E 0.1) and one strong cash year (FY-3, +₹11,019m), so survival is not the question — value creation at these returns is.

governance.reasoning: The Company is a SEBI-registered Investment Adviser that has itself been fined by SEBI (₹4 lakh) and received show cause notices from SEBI, including one as recent as 2025 — a regulator sanctioning a regulated intermediary is not a trivial footnote. Extracts also show related-party arrangements (including collateral and bank guarantees against related balances) but nothing establishing them as abusive, so I score this as a real negative flag, not fraud.

key_risks.why_it_matters: Operating cash flow was negative in the two most recent years while PAT was strongly positive, so the earnings quality underpinning the IPO price is questionable.
Collection period went from 35 to 137 days in two years; either customers cannot/will not pay on time or revenue is being booked ahead of cash.
A SEBI penalty on the Company and open show cause notices against a SEBI-registered adviser create direct compliance and licence risk to the core business.
Revenue fell ~24% and ROE fell to 7.6% in the latest year, so the business being sold is deteriorating, which is the classic 'priced for the seller' setup.

answers.question: where did the money go — receivables, inventory, or both?
answers.answer: Receivables, at minimum: collection days jumped from 35.3 to 137.2 over two years, which matches the swing from +₹11,019m operating cash flow to -₹1,970m. Whether inventory also absorbed cash is not visible — no inventory figure or working-capital passage was given to me, so 'both' cannot be confirmed or excluded.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: The basis-for-ipo-price chapter with peer valuation, the fresh-issue/OFS split, and a receivables ageing/dispute note — if pricing came out at a low multiple of even the depressed latest-year earnings, or if receivables proved to be a one-off timing item fully collected post-year-end, my longterm score would rise materially.
